What drives bottled-water sales, and what is media worth?¶

Marketing mix model for an FMCG bottled-water brand¶

Author: Yazan Alrefaai  ·  Date: October 2026  ·  Data: 161 weeks, Jan 2022 - Jan 2025

Question. Help an FMCG bottled-water brand understand how effective its media is at driving sales, and identify the other key drivers of sales.

Contents

  1. Load and check the data
  2. Sales, seasonality and weather
  3. Price, promotions and distribution
  4. Media and competitors
  5. Model: log-linear regression with media carryover (adstock) and diminishing returns (saturation)
  6. Validation: strict holdout, residual diagnostics, multicollinearity, stability, sensitivity
  7. Results: decomposition, media ROI, response curves, year-on-year bridge, promotions
  8. Conclusions and next steps

The model engine is in src/mmm.py; every modelling decision and its reason is in docs/decision_log.md.

Executive summary¶

Model quality. Adjusted R² 0.91; average weekly error 4.5%; error on 12 unseen weeks 4.2% (whole pipeline re-run without them).

What drives volume. Base sales (brand, price, distribution) 79%, weather 20%, media 0.8%.

Driver Effect on weekly volume
+1°C max temperature +1.9% (and +2.2% more per °C above 20°C)
+10 mm rain -1.7%
Christmas / New Year week -22%
+10% price vs competitors -4.3%
+1 point weighted distribution +3.7%

Media. All modelled media returned £1.53 of revenue per £1.

Channel Spend ROI (revenue per £1) 95% range Next £1 returns
OOH £350k £5.35 £0.00 - £13.18 £2.95
Online partnership £575k £3.07 £1.65 - £4.52 £2.22
Online video £1,250k £0.29 £0.00 - £5.42 £0.20
TV £529k £0.27 £0.00 - £0.90 £0.10

Social, Search and RDM could not be measured (wrong sign or too little spend).

Year on year. Volume -5.9% in 2023, mainly relative price (-8.1 pts); +7.1% in 2024, mainly distribution (+12.8 pts).

Promotions. About 28% of promoted volume is incremental; promotions work by widening store reach, not through discount depth.

Sanity checks on definitions¶

If the data is consistent, promo sales should never exceed total sales, and value / volume should equal the average price per kg.

In [5]:
checks = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "promo_vol_gt_total": df["Promotion_Volume_Sales"] > df["Volume_Sales"],
        "price_mismatch": (df["Value_Sales"] / df["Volume_Sales"] - df["Avg_PPKG"]).abs() > 0.01,
    }
)
print("Weeks failing each check:", checks.sum().to_dict())

# Average pack size (kg per unit) tells us what product we are looking at
print("Avg kg per unit:", (df["Volume_Sales"] / df["Unit_Sales"]).describe().round(2).to_dict())

Step 2 - Sales, seasonality and weather¶

Questions: How big is the brand? Is it growing? When does it sell? How much does the weather matter for bottled water?

In [7]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from style import INK_2, MUTED, SERIES, load, save, thousands

df = load()
df["Year"] = df["Date"].dt.year
df["Month"] = df["Date"].dt.month
# Week number from day of year (ISO weeks would put 1 Jan 2022 in week 52)
df["Week"] = (df["Date"].dt.dayofyear - 1) // 7 + 1

Size and growth per year¶

2025 has only 4 weeks, so it is excluded from yearly comparisons.

In [8]:
full_years = df[df["Year"] < 2025]
yearly = full_years.groupby("Year").agg(
    weeks=("Date", "count"),
    volume_kg=("Volume_Sales", "sum"),
    value_gbp=("Value_Sales", "sum"),
    promo_volume=("Promotion_Volume_Sales", "sum"),
    avg_price_kg=("Avg_PPKG", "mean"),
    avg_temp=("weather_average_temp", "mean"),
)
yearly["promo_share"] = yearly["promo_volume"] / yearly["volume_kg"]
# 2022 has 53 weekly rows and 2023/2024 have 52, so compare average weeks, not totals
yearly["avg_week_volume"] = yearly["volume_kg"] / yearly["weeks"]
yearly["avg_week_value"] = yearly["value_gbp"] / yearly["weeks"]
yearly["volume_growth"] = yearly["avg_week_volume"].pct_change()
yearly["value_growth"] = yearly["avg_week_value"].pct_change()
print(yearly.round(3).to_string())

x, y = df["weather_max_temp"], df["Volume_Sales"]

df["promo_share"] = df["Promotion_Volume_Sales"] / df["Volume_Sales"]

Step 4 - Media and competitors¶

Questions: How much was spent per channel, and when? Which channels run at the same time (hard for a model to separate)? What are competitors doing?

In [23]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from style import INK_2, SERIES, load, save, thousands

df = load()

CHANNELS = ["TV", "VOD", "OLV", "Social", "Search", "RDM", "Online_Partnership", "OOH"]
spend_cols = {c: f"Media_{c}_Spends" for c in CHANNELS}
activity_cols = {
    "TV": "Media_TV_GRPs",
    "VOD": "Media_VOD_Impressions",
    "OLV": "Media_OLV_Impressions",
    "Social": "Media_Social_Impressions",
    "Search": "Media_Search_Impressions",
    "RDM": "Media_RDM_Impressions",
}

Budget summary per channel¶

In [24]:
rows = []
for c, col in spend_cols.items():
    s = df[col]
    on = s > 0
    rows.append(
        {
            "channel": c,
            "total_spend": s.sum(),
            "active_weeks": int(on.sum()),
            "first_week": df.loc[on, "Date"].min().date(),
            "last_week": df.loc[on, "Date"].max().date(),
            "avg_spend_when_on": s[on].mean(),
        }
    )
summary = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("channel").sort_values("total_spend", ascending=False)
summary["share_of_budget"] = summary["total_spend"] / summary["total_spend"].sum()
print(summary.round(2).to_string())
print("\nTotal media spend: £{:,.0f}".format(summary["total_spend"].sum()))
print("Total value sales: £{:,.0f}".format(df["Value_Sales"].sum()))

# Cost per thousand impressions (CPM) / cost per GRP, where activity exists
for c, col in activity_cols.items():
    on = df[spend_cols[c]] > 0
    cost = df.loc[on, spend_cols[c]].sum() / df.loc[on, col].sum()
    unit = "per GRP" if c == "TV" else "per 1,000 impressions"
    print(f"{c:7s} cost {unit}: £{cost * (1 if c == 'TV' else 1000):,.2f}")

Step 5 - Build the model¶

We add drivers one group at a time and watch how much each one explains. Then we choose media carryover rates and fit the final model.

In [31]:
import json

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson

import mmm
from style import ROOT, SERIES, load, save, thousands

df = load()
y = np.log(df["Volume_Sales"])
X_base = mmm.base_features(df)
OUT = ROOT / "outputs"

Model-building journey¶

Each stage adds a group of drivers. Adjusted R² only rises if a driver explains more than it costs in complexity.

In [32]:
stages = [
    ("1. Temperature only", ["max_temp"]),
    ("2. + hot weeks, rain, Christmas", ["max_temp", "hot_degrees", "rainfall", "xmas_week"]),
    ("3. + relative price", ["max_temp", "hot_degrees", "rainfall", "xmas_week", "ln_relative_price"]),
    ("4. + distribution", mmm.BASE_DRIVERS),
]
journey = []
for name, cols in stages:
    res = mmm.fit_ols(y, X_base[cols])
    journey.append(
        {
            "stage": name,
            "adj_R2": res.rsquared_adj,
            "MAPE": mmm.mape(df["Volume_Sales"], np.exp(res.fittedvalues)),
            "DW": durbin_watson(res.resid),
            "AIC": res.aic,
        }
    )

Media carryover (adstock) rates¶

Grid search over business-sense ranges; keep the best AIC where all media effects are positive.

In [33]:
channels = list(mmm.MEDIA)
rates = mmm.search_adstock(df, y, X_base, channels)
print("Chosen weekly carryover rates:", rates)
half_life = {ch: (np.log(0.5) / np.log(r) if r > 0 else 0) for ch, r in rates.items()}
print("Half-life in weeks:", {k: round(float(v), 1) for k, v in half_life.items()})

model = mmm.MMM(df, rates)
res = model.res
journey.append(
    {
        "stage": "5. + media (final model)",
        "adj_R2": res.rsquared_adj,
        "MAPE": mmm.mape(df["Volume_Sales"], model.predict()),
        "DW": durbin_watson(res.resid),
        "AIC": res.aic,
    }
)
journey = pd.DataFrame(journey)
print(journey.round(3).to_string(index=False))

2. + hot weeks, rain, Christmas   0.722 0.085 0.565 -257.196

Final model coefficients¶

How to read them (log model):

  • a unit driver: +1 unit changes volume by about (exp(coef) - 1) %
  • ln(relative price): the coefficient is the price elasticity
  • media: effect in an average on-air week (adstock = its scale, so log(1 + 1) = 0.69)
In [34]:
print(res.summary())

coef = pd.DataFrame({"coef": res.params, "std_err": res.bse, "t": res.tvalues, "p_value": res.pvalues})
effects = {
    "max_temp": ("+1°C", np.exp(res.params["max_temp"]) - 1),
    "hot_degrees": (f"+1°C above {mmm.HOT_THRESHOLD}°C (extra)", np.exp(res.params["hot_degrees"]) - 1),
    "rainfall": ("+10 mm rain", np.exp(10 * res.params["rainfall"]) - 1),
    "xmas_week": ("Christmas / New Year week", np.exp(res.params["xmas_week"]) - 1),
    "ln_relative_price": ("+10% price vs competitors", 1.1 ** res.params["ln_relative_price"] - 1),
    "distribution_acv": ("+1 point ACV distribution", np.exp(res.params["distribution_acv"]) - 1),
}
for ch in channels:
    effects[ch] = ("average on-air week", np.exp(res.params[ch] * np.log(2)) - 1)
coef["meaning"] = [effects.get(i, ("", np.nan))[0] for i in coef.index]
coef["volume_effect"] = [effects.get(i, ("", np.nan))[1] for i in coef.index]
coef["confidence"] = pd.cut(coef["t"].abs(), [0, 1, 2, np.inf], labels=["low", "medium", "high"])
print(coef.round(4).to_string())

Variables tested and rejected¶

Each candidate is added on top of the final model to show why it is not in it.

    .where(share >= 0.05, 0)
    .clip(lower=0),

            mmm.adstock(df["Comp_Brand_A_Media_Spends"].to_numpy(float), 0.5),

    ),
    "Competitor B media": pd.Series(
        mmm.saturate(

        index=df.index,

}
for ch, r in [("Social", 0.3), ("Search", 0.3), ("RDM", 0.3)]:

    candidates[f"{ch} media"] = pd.Series(
        mmm.saturate(mmm.adstock(s, r), mmm.saturation_scale(s, r)), index=df.index
    )

rejected = []

            "t": r.tvalues["candidate"],
            "adj_R2_with": r.rsquared_adj,
            "adj_R2_without": res.rsquared_adj,
        }
    )
rejected = pd.DataFrame(rejected)

Step 6 - Can we trust the model?¶

  1. Holdout test: fit without the last 12 weeks, then predict them.
  2. Residual checks: errors should look like random noise.
  3. Multicollinearity (VIF).
  4. Stability: do the main coefficients hold if we drop a year?
  5. Sensitivity: how much do key results move under reasonable alternatives?
In [38]:
import json

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_breusch_godfrey, het_breuschpagan
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson, jarque_bera

import mmm
from style import INK_2, MUTED, ROOT, SERIES, load, save, thousands

df = load()
OUT = ROOT / "outputs"
rates = json.loads((OUT / "model_config.json").read_text())["rates"]
model = mmm.MMM(df, rates)
res = model.res

1. Holdout test (last 12 weeks)¶

The whole pipeline is re-run on the first 149 weeks only: carryover search, saturation scales and coefficients. The last 12 weeks are never seen.

In [39]:
HOLDOUT = 12
train = df.index < len(df) - HOLDOUT
train_df = df[train].reset_index(drop=True)
y_all = np.log(df["Volume_Sales"])

rates_train = (
    mmm.search_adstock(
        train_df, np.log(train_df["Volume_Sales"]), mmm.base_features(train_df), list(mmm.MEDIA)
    )
    or rates
)
scales_train = {}
for ch, r in rates_train.items():
    a = mmm.adstock(mmm.channel_spend(df, ch), r)[train]
    scales_train[ch] = a[a > 0].mean()
X_all = pd.concat([mmm.base_features(df), mmm.media_features(df, rates_train, scales_train)], axis=1)

res_train = mmm.fit_ols(y_all[train], X_all[train])
smear = np.mean(np.exp(res_train.resid))
pred_all = np.exp(res_train.params["const"] + X_all @ res_train.params[X_all.columns]) * smear
print("Carryover rates chosen on training weeks:", rates_train, "(full data:", rates, ")")

mape_train = mmm.mape(df.loc[train, "Volume_Sales"], pred_all[train])
mape_test = mmm.mape(df.loc[~train, "Volume_Sales"], pred_all[~train])
bias_test = (pred_all[~train].sum() / df.loc[~train, "Volume_Sales"].sum()) - 1
print(
    f"Training MAPE: {mape_train:.1%}   Holdout MAPE: {mape_test:.1%}   Holdout total bias: {bias_test:+.1%}"
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
ax.plot(df["Date"], df["Volume_Sales"], color=SERIES[0], label="Actual")
ax.plot(df["Date"][train], pred_all[train], color=SERIES[1], linewidth=1.6, label="Model (training weeks)")
ax.plot(
    df["Date"][~train],
    pred_all[~train],
    color=SERIES[1],
    linewidth=2,
    linestyle="--",
    label="Model forecast (holdout)",
)
ax.axvspan(df["Date"][~train].min(), df["Date"].max(), color=MUTED, alpha=0.12, linewidth=0)
ax.set_title(f"Holdout test: model forecasts unseen last 12 weeks with {mape_test:.1%} average error")
ax.set_ylim(0)
thousands(ax)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=3)
save(fig, "12_holdout_test")

Carryover rates chosen on training weeks: {'TV': 0.3, 'Online video': 0.8, 'Online partnership': 0.0, 'OOH': 0.5} (full data: {'TV': 0.3, 'Online video': 0.8, 'Online partnership': 0.0, 'OOH': 0.5} )
Training MAPE: 4.5%   Holdout MAPE: 4.2%   Holdout total bias: +1.7%

2. Residual checks¶

  • Durbin-Watson ~2 means no week-to-week correlation in errors (below 2 = positive correlation).
  • Breusch-Godfrey: formal test for autocorrelation (small p = autocorrelation present).
  • Breusch-Pagan: are errors bigger in some weeks than others? (small p = yes).
  • Jarque-Bera: are errors normally distributed? (small p = no).
In [40]:
resid = res.resid
X_const = sm.add_constant(model.X)
ols_plain = sm.OLS(model.y, X_const).fit()
bg = acorr_breusch_godfrey(ols_plain, nlags=4, result_object=False)
bp = het_breuschpagan(resid, X_const)
jb = jarque_bera(resid)
diagnostics = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"check": "Durbin-Watson", "value": durbin_watson(resid), "p_value": np.nan},
        {"check": "Breusch-Godfrey (4 lags)", "value": bg[0], "p_value": bg[1]},
        {"check": "Breusch-Pagan", "value": bp[0], "p_value": bp[1]},
        {"check": "Jarque-Bera", "value": jb[0], "p_value": jb[1]},
        {"check": "Residual std (log points)", "value": resid.std(), "p_value": np.nan},
    ]
)
print(diagnostics.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("Autocorrelation of residuals, lags 1-4:", [round(float(resid.autocorr(k)), 2) for k in range(1, 5)])

largest = (
    pd.DataFrame({"Date": df["Date"], "resid_pct": np.exp(resid) - 1})
    .reindex(resid.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
    .head(6)
)
print("Largest misses (actual vs model):\n", largest.to_string(index=False, float_format="%.3f"))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3, 1]})
ax1.bar(df["Date"], (np.exp(resid) - 1) * 100, width=6, color=SERIES[0])
ax1.axhline(0, color=INK_2, linewidth=0.8)
ax1.set_title("Model error by week (% actual vs model): no clear pattern left")
ax2.hist(resid * 100, bins=20, color=SERIES[0], edgecolor="white")
ax2.set_title("Error distribution (%)", fontsize=10, color=INK_2)

3. Multicollinearity (VIF)¶

VIF above ~5-10 means a variable is largely explained by the others, so its own coefficient is unreliable.

Step 7 - Results: what drives sales, and what does media return?¶

  1. Decomposition: weekly volume split into base, weather, Christmas and media.
  2. Media: incremental volume, revenue and ROI per channel (with a range).
  3. Response curves: what happens if spend per channel goes up or down.
  4. Year-on-year bridge: why volume fell in 2023 and recovered in 2024.
  5. Promotions: their effect works through distribution.
In [45]:

2. Media incremental volume, revenue and ROI¶

ROI = incremental revenue (£) / spend (£). Revenue ROI, not profit: we have no margin data. Range: re-computed with the coefficient at its 95% confidence bounds (floored at zero).

In [47]:
spend = model.actual_spend()
rows = []
for ch in channels:
    inc = model.channel_incremental(ch)
    lo_coef = max(b[ch] - 1.96 * model.res.bse[ch], 0)
    hi_coef = b[ch] + 1.96 * model.res.bse[ch]
    inc_lo = model.channel_incremental(ch, coef=lo_coef)
    inc_hi = model.channel_incremental(ch, coef=hi_coef)
    total_spend = spend[ch].sum()
    rows.append(
        {
            "channel": ch,
            "spend": total_spend,
            "incremental_kg": inc.sum(),
            "incremental_revenue": (inc * price).sum(),
            "roi": (inc * price).sum() / total_spend,
            "roi_low": (inc_lo * price).sum() / total_spend,
            "roi_high": (inc_hi * price).sum() / total_spend,
            "t_stat": model.res.tvalues[ch],
            "carryover_rate": rates[ch],
        }
    )
media = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("channel")
media["share_of_spend"] = media["spend"] / media["spend"].sum()
media["share_of_media_volume"] = media["incremental_kg"] / media["incremental_kg"].sum()

)

3. Response curves¶

Scale each channel's actual weekly plan (same weeks, same shape) from 0x to 3x and measure incremental revenue. The slope at 1x is the marginal ROI: what the NEXT £1 would return.

In [48]:
multipliers = np.linspace(0, 3, 31)
curves = {}
for ch in channels:
    rev = []
    for k in multipliers:
        s = {**spend, ch: spend[ch] * k}
        rev.append((model.channel_incremental(ch, spend=s) * price).sum())
    curves[ch] = pd.Series(rev, index=multipliers * spend[ch].sum())
for ch in channels:
    s = {**spend, ch: spend[ch] * 1.1}
    extra = (model.channel_incremental(ch, spend=s) * price).sum() - media.loc[ch, "incremental_revenue"]
    media.loc[ch, "marginal_roi"] = extra / (0.1 * spend[ch].sum())
print(media[["roi", "marginal_roi"]].round(2).to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for ch in channels:
    c = curves[ch]
    ax.plot(c.index, c.values, color=colors[ch], label=ch)

Budget scenarios (same total budget)¶

Move 30% of the TV and Online video budgets (lowest marginal ROI) into the channels with the highest marginal ROI. New money is added in the weeks those channels already ran, in proportion to their existing plan.

In [49]:
def move_budget(source, target, pct=0.3):
    moved = {ch: pct * spend[ch] for ch in source}
    amount = sum(v.sum() for v in moved.values())
    new = {ch: spend[ch] - moved.get(ch, 0) for ch in channels}
    new[target] = spend[target] + amount * spend[target] / spend[target].sum()
    delta = ((model.predict(model.with_spend(new)) - model.predict(model.with_spend(spend))) * price).sum()
    return amount, delta


scenarios = {}
for target in ["Online partnership", "OOH"]:
    amount, delta = move_budget(["TV", "Online video"], target)
    scenarios[target] = {"moved": amount, "delta_revenue": delta}
    print(
        f"Move £{amount:,.0f} from TV + Online video into {target}: revenue {delta:+,.0f} "
        f"({delta / media['incremental_revenue'].sum():+.0%} of media-driven revenue)"
    )

Move £533,719 from TV + Online video into OOH: revenue +1,046,128 (+25% of media-driven revenue)

4. Year-on-year bridge¶

In a log model, the change in average log volume splits exactly into coefficient x change in each driver's average. 100 x log points ~ % change.

In [50]:
yr = df["Date"].dt.year
groups = {
    "Weather": ["max_temp", "hot_degrees", "rainfall"],
    "Christmas timing": ["xmas_week"],
    "Relative price": ["ln_relative_price"],
    "Distribution": ["distribution_acv"],
    "Media": channels,
}
means = model.X.groupby(yr).mean()
resid_mean = model.res.resid.groupby(yr).mean()
bridge = {}
for a, c in [(2022, 2023), (2023, 2024)]:
    row = {g: 100 * sum(b[v] * (means.loc[c, v] - means.loc[a, v]) for v in vs) for g, vs in groups.items()}
    row["Unexplained"] = 100 * (resid_mean[c] - resid_mean[a])
    row["Total (log pts)"] = 100 * (
        np.log(df.loc[yr == c, "Volume_Sales"]).mean() - np.log(df.loc[yr == a, "Volume_Sales"]).mean()
    )
    bridge[f"{a}->{c}"] = row
bridge = pd.DataFrame(bridge)
print(bridge.round(1).to_string())
print(
    "Driver averages by year:\n",
    means[["max_temp", "hot_degrees", "rainfall", "ln_relative_price", "distribution_acv"]]
    .round(3)
    .to_string(),
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, col in zip(axes, bridge.columns, strict=True):
    vals = bridge[col].drop("Total (log pts)")
    cols = [SERIES[0] if v >= 0 else SERIES[7] for v in vals]
    ax.barh(vals.index[::-1], vals.values[::-1], color=cols[::-1], height=0.55)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals.values[::-1]):
        ax.annotate(
            f"{v:+.1f}",
            (v, i),
            xytext=(4 if v >= 0 else -4, 0),
            textcoords="offset points",
            ha="left" if v >= 0 else "right",
            va="center",
            fontsize=9,
            color=INK_2,
        )
    ax.axvline(0, color=INK_2, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_title(
        f"{col.replace('->', ' to ')}: volume {bridge.loc['Total (log pts)', col]:+.1f}%", fontsize=11
    )
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    lim = (
        max(abs(bridge.drop("Total (log pts)").values.min()), bridge.drop("Total (log pts)").values.max())
        * 1.4
    )
    ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim)
fig.suptitle(
    "Why volume changed year on year (contribution, ~% points)", x=0.01, y=1.02, ha="left", fontweight="bold"
)

5. Promotions work through distribution¶

In the model, promo variables add nothing once distribution is included. But promotions raise distribution: more stores sell the product when it is on deal.

In [51]:
link = sm.OLS(
    df["ACV_Weighted_Distribution_wtd"],
    sm.add_constant(
        pd.DataFrame(
            {"promo_acv": df["Promotion_ACV_Weighted_Distribution_wtd"], "trend": np.arange(len(df)) / 52}
        )
    ),
).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 4})
per_point = link.params["promo_acv"]
promo_effect_per_point = np.exp(per_point * b["distribution_acv"]) - 1
avg_promo_acv = df["Promotion_ACV_Weighted_Distribution_wtd"].mean()
promo_total = np.exp(per_point * b["distribution_acv"] * avg_promo_acv) - 1
print(
    f"+1 point promo ACV -> +{per_point:.2f} points total ACV (t {link.tvalues['promo_acv']:.1f}) "
    f"-> +{promo_effect_per_point:.2%} volume"
)
print(
    f"Average promo ACV {avg_promo_acv:.1f} points -> promotions lift volume "
    f"~{promo_total:.1%} via distribution"
)
promo_share = df["Promotion_Volume_Sales"].sum() / df["Volume_Sales"].sum()
print(f"Share of volume sold on promotion: {promo_share:.1%}")
print(
    f"=> about {promo_total / (1 + promo_total) / promo_share:.0%} of promoted volume looks incremental; "
    "the rest would have sold at full price"
)

depth_by_year = (
    (1 - df["Promotion_Avg_PPKG"] / df["Base_Avg_PPKG"])
    .where(df["Promotion_Volume_Sales"] / df["Volume_Sales"] >= 0.05)
    .groupby(yr)
    .mean()
)
print("Average promo discount by year:", (depth_by_year * 100).round(1).to_dict())

8. Conclusions and next steps¶

Recommendations

  1. Grow distribution - the strongest controllable lever (+3.7% volume per ACV point).
  2. Manage the price gap to competitors - the widening premium explains most of the 2023 volume decline.
  3. Rebalance media - moving 30% of the TV and online video budget (£534k) into Online partnership adds about £0.9M revenue at the same total spend. Test OOH regionally before scaling it; if TV continues, spread it over more weeks.
  4. Rethink promotions - test shallower discounts and focus on store reach.

Limitations

  • TV ran 3 weeks and OOH 5 weeks, so their ROIs carry wide ranges; several channels overlap in time.
  • ROI is revenue-based (no margin data) and short-term (no long-term brand effects).
  • The price elasticity is sensitive to adding a time trend (-0.46 without, -0.10 with).
  • Week-to-week correlation in residuals is handled with Newey-West robust standard errors.

Next steps

  • Bayesian MMM (e.g. Google Meridian, PyMC-Marketing) with priors to stabilise sparse channels.
  • Regional or retailer-level data, and lift tests to calibrate OOH and Online partnership.
  • Margin data for profit ROI; store-level promotion evaluation.
